frameworks.definition: Intent and impact are two separate things that can run in any combination. Confusing them produces two failure modes: inventing the other person's intent (usually worse than real) on the receiving end, and using good intent to excuse bad impact on the delivering end.
Inventing the other person's intent — almost always worse than the real intent — and reacting to the invented version as if it were confirmed.
Using 'I didn't mean it' as if it resolved the impact. Intent and impact are separate. A defense of intent does not address the impact the other person already experienced.

Hold intent and impact separately. Acknowledge the impact as real without using it as evidence for harmful intent. Name the intent without using it to close the impact conversation. Sequence: impact acknowledgment before intent explanation.

anchors.label: Manager offhand comment (Kai/Miriam)
anchors.description: Manager makes an accent joke; junior engineer messages that evening saying it made her uncomfortable. Manager's first response is 'I didn't mean anything by it' — sincere and counterproductive.
anchors.friction: Each additional intent explanation makes engineer feel more dismissed
anchors.consequence: Working relationship cooled; engineer avoiding one-on-ones

anchors.label: Partner cancellations (Hayden/Soleil)
anchors.description: Three cancellations; partner says it feels like Hayden doesn't want to spend time together. Hayden responds with intent statement, not impact acknowledgment.
anchors.friction: Intent defense does not address impact; partner hears it as another dismissal

anchors.label: Email omission
anchors.description: Volunteer leaves colleague off email chain about a decision affecting their work. Colleague finds out at team meeting, in front of others. Volunteer keeps explaining 'honest mistake.'
anchors.friction: Colleague not questioning intent; experiencing impact of exclusion. Explanation keeps missing the point.
anchors.consequence: Two weeks of coldness between them

limits: The disentangle move primarily addresses unintentional harm — the asymmetric case (genuine harmful intent) makes the move more demanding, not easier
Acknowledging impact does not mean accepting blame for intent — the two are separate, and the chapter does not fully resolve the language for holding both
In high-power-gap contexts, acknowledging impact without defending intent can expose the less-powerful party to retaliation
